newsitem.title: USA: U.S. denounces Peruvian courts trying rebels.
newsitem.headline: U.S. denounces Peruvian courts trying rebels.

text.p: The U.S. State Department on Thursday denounced Peru in its annual human rights report for secretly trying rebels in closed military courts, but said its criticism should not impede the release of 72 hostages held by Marxist guerrillas in Lima.

"Proceedings in military courts that hear terrorism and treason cases do not meet internationally accepted standards for due process," the department said in the Peru chapter of its human rights survey of 193 nations.
Military trials of such guerrillas are closed to the public and are carried out in secrecy by military judges whose identities are not revealed in court, the State Department said.

The report was released at a delicate time. Six weeks ago leftist Tupac Amaru rebels invaded a party at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, taking more than 500 hostages. Although many have since been released, there has been no movement toward a resolution of the crisis.
The rebels have highlighted the treatment of their fellow rebels in the Peruvian justice system and are demanding freedom for 400 jailed comrades -- a demand Peru has refused to discuss.
The State Department said Peruvian defence attorneys were denied access to evidence and were unable to interview police or military witnesses before or during a trial to protect their identities.

The report said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement and the Maoist Sendero Luminoso (Shining Path) guerrilla movements continued to pose a security threat in some areas, "but at a much reduced level than in previous years."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said he did not expect criticism of the "faceless" military tribunals to undermine President Alberto Fujimori's efforts to free the hostages.
"I don't believe this should have any impact whatsoever on our hope for a successful early and peaceful release of all the hostages," he said.
Fujimori and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will meet in Toronto on Saturday to discuss ways to resolve the hostage crisis.

Fujimori has ruled out giving in to the Tupac Amaru rebels' demands, even though his brother Pedro is one of the hostages. After the Toronto talks, he will arrive in Washington on Saturday for possible meetings with U.S. leaders and will speak at the National Press Club on Monday, the Peruvian embassy said.
Burns said the United States had longstanding concerns about the "faceless" courts.
"We've made them public. We have an obligation to make them public," he said in reply to a question at his regular briefing, referring to cases of U.S. citizens who have been tried by such courts.

Lori Berenson, a 27-year-old freelance journalist from New York, was sentenced to life imprisonment a year ago on treason and terrorism charges stemming from her involvement with the Tupac Amaru guerrillas. She was tried in a closed court by military judges who wore hoods. Authorities rejected her requests for an open trial in a civilian court.
In October the Peruvian authorities extended for another year trials by faceless courts, "further undermining fairness, due process and accountability," the State Department report said.
